MARKET ATTRACTIVENESS: Moderate-to-weak as currently framed. The broad candle market is large, but the venture's serviceable market is much narrower: small/independent candle makers who (a) use reusable-grade glass jars, (b) ship direct-to-consumer, and (c) will pay per-jar fees plus coordinate refill logistics. No TAM/SAM/SOM, jar-volume math, or maker counts are provided ('thousands' of makers, 'a very large number of jars' are unsupported assertions). A rough sanity check: a typical micro-maker sells perhaps a few hundred to a few thousand candles per year, and return rates for consumer reuse programs are historically low (often single digits to low teens percent even with incentives), so jar throughput per maker could be only tens to low hundreds per year. That implies thousands of partner makers would be needed to reach meaningful volume, with each paying a small per-jar fee. Sustainability tailwinds are real, but they do not substitute for sizing.

WOULD THE MARKET SUPPORT THIS VENTURE: Uncertain; the unit economics are the central question. Reverse logistics for a heavy, fragile, low-value item is punishing: a glass jar costs roughly $1-3 new in bulk, while a prepaid return label, mailer, inbound handling, de-waxing, washing, inspection, breakage losses, and return shipping to the maker likely exceed that substantially. The claim that a per-jar fee will undercut buying new jars is unlikely to hold at small scale, and probably not even at large scale, because postage is a fixed physical cost that does not decline with volume the way the plan assumes. The value proposition therefore depends on makers paying a premium for sustainability marketing, not on cost savings. That is a narrower, more fragile demand driver. The plan itself identifies the strongest competitor correctly: customer inaction. Return-rate risk is existential, since low returns mean low volume, high per-jar overhead, and weak dashboard data. Also noteworthy: wax residue, label/adhesive variability, and mixed jar types across makers complicate standardized processing, and local-pickup/drop-off or maker-run refill-in-store models can undercut mail-based solutions.

TARGETING THE CORRECT GROUP: Partially. Small makers are a sensible beachhead because large brands run in-house programs and are hard to sell to, and these makers are values-aligned and lack bandwidth. However, there are two weaknesses. First, small makers are also the least able to pay, the most price-sensitive, and the most fragmented, which means high customer-acquisition cost per account and low revenue per account. Second, the plan has two customers (makers and eco-minded gift buyers) without clarity on who is the economic buyer versus the end user; consumers are the behavior-change bottleneck but are not the primary payer. The 'eco-minded gift buyer' segment is also somewhat mismatched: gift recipients, not purchasers, are the ones who must return the jar, and recipients are not necessarily eco-motivated. A tighter initial focus would be a dense geographic cluster of local makers with a regional drop-off/pickup model, which could validate return rates and cost per jar before committing to national mail logistics. Alternatively, targeting mid-size DTC candle brands, who have larger volumes and bigger sustainability marketing budgets, may offer better revenue per account.

SCALABILITY: Limited by structure. Revenue scales linearly with jars processed, while costs (labor, postage, breakage, space) scale nearly linearly too; economies of scale exist in cleaning labor and bulk mailers but are capped by shipping costs. Growth would require physical processing capacity, likely regional hubs to manage freight, and consistent maker coordination. The dashboard is the only genuinely scalable, high-margin component, but standing alone it is a thin, easily replicated feature. Operational complexity (sanitation standards, inspection, inventory flow between makers and processor) also grows with each partner. A path to scale likely involves expanding beyond candles to other reusable glass/container categories (balms, jars, cosmetics), or becoming a platform/infrastructure layer for small brands, but the plan does not articulate this.

EXIT POTENTIAL: Low-to-modest in the base case. This resembles a small, operations-heavy service business rather than a venture-scale software or marketplace play, which reduces the likelihood of a large strategic exit or IPO. Plausible exits: (1) acquisition by a reuse/circular-packaging platform (e.g., companies in the reusable packaging space) seeking a niche vertical or customer list, (2) acquisition by a large candle or home-fragrance brand or a supplier of candle vessels wanting a sustainability program, or (3) lifestyle/cash-flow business with the founders as operators. Acqui-hire or tuck-in valuations would likely be small given thin margins and no proprietary technology or IP. Upside increases materially only if the company builds a defensible network (many makers, standardized vessel program, brand-neutral reusable jar) or expands to a multi-category reuse infrastructure, which would make it more attractive to larger circular-economy players. The team's student status and part-time commitment, the lack of a legal entity, and the lack of validated unit economics further lower near-term exit credibility.

OVERALL: An appealing, values-driven concept with genuine pain points, but market sizing is absent, the serviceable market is narrower than implied, the unit economics are doubtful, and exit prospects are modest. Priorities: (1) build a bottom-up model of jars per maker, return rate, and fully loaded cost per returned jar; (2) run a measured pilot to establish actual return rates and willingness to pay; (3) test a local/regional model before national mail; (4) clarify the economic buyer; and (5) explore expanding to additional container categories to improve scale and strategic value.

Business plan text:

Wickedgood Candle Return
Wickedgood Candle Return
Executive Summary
Problem
Candles are a popular product, especially as gifts, but when a candle is finished the jar is
usually thrown in the trash. Many candle jars are made of good quality glass that could be used
many more times. Because there is no easy way to send them back, most people either throw them
out or keep a few around the house as storage. This creates unnecessary waste and is a growing
concern for people who care about the environment. At the same time, small candle makers want
to be more sustainable but they are busy making and selling candles. They do not have the time,
space, or money to set up their own system for collecting, cleaning and reusing jars. Customers
who want to do the right thing also have no easy way to see the impact of their choices. We
believe this is a real problem that affects both buyers and sellers of candles.
Solution
Wickedgood Candle Return is a reuse program that makes returning candle jars simple. Our
solution has three parts.
First, a prepaid mailer. A candle maker who partners with us includes a prepaid return mailer
in the box with each candle order, or customers can request one from us. When the candle is
finished the customer puts the empty jar in the mailer and drops it in the mail.
Second, cleaning and refilling. When jars arrive at our workspace we remove leftover wax, wash
and sanitize the glass, inspect it for chips and cracks, and then send good jars back to the
candle maker, who refills them with fresh wax and sells them again.
Third, a data dashboard. Each customer and each candle maker can log in to see how many jars
have been returned, how much glass waste was avoided, and an estimate of the carbon saved. We
think this makes the impact feel real and gives candle makers something to share with their own
customers.
Market
The candle market is large and growing. Candles are sold in grocery stores, gift shops, online
shops and at craft markets. Our focus is on two groups. The first is eco-minded gift buyers,
who often choose products based on values and are willing to pay a bit more for something
sustainable. The second is small and independent candle makers, who number in the thousands
across the country and sell mostly online and at local markets. We estimate that if even a
small share of these makers joined our program, we could handle a very large number of jars
each year. We have not yet done a detailed market sizing, but we believe the growing interest
in sustainability and reuse means demand will continue to increase.
Business Model
We plan to make money in a few ways. Candle makers would pay us a fee for each jar that is
returned, cleaned and sent back to them. Customers may also pay a small fee for the mailer when
it is not included by the candle maker. In the future we could offer premium dashboard features
to candle makers, such as more detailed reports they can use in marketing. We have not
finalized our prices. Our early thinking is that a fee per jar would be lower than the cost of
buying new jars, which would make the program attractive to candle makers, but we still need to
test this. Our costs include the mailers, postage, cleaning supplies, labor and the software
for the dashboard. We expect that as we handle more jars our cost per jar will come down.
Competition
There are other reuse and return programs in the market, and some larger candle brands have

started offering refills for their own products. There are also general packaging reuse
services that work with many kinds of products. What makes us different is that we focus only
on candles and on small makers, and we include a data dashboard so that customers can see their
impact. We believe a focused service is easier for small makers to use than a general one.
Large brands run their own programs and are not likely to serve small makers. We think our
biggest competition is really customers doing nothing, because returning a jar takes effort and
many people will not bother.
Team
Maya Lindqvist is a junior studying environmental science and leads operations and
partnerships. She has experience running a campus recycling drive. Derrick Okonkwo-Hale is a
senior studying industrial design and leads the physical product, including the mailer and the
cleaning process. Priya Venkataraman is a junior studying information systems and builds the
dashboard and handles the data. We are all students at our university and work on this
alongside our classes. We have not yet added any advisors, but we plan to look for mentors with
experience in consumer products and logistics.
Milestones and Financials
So far we have defined our core business concept, built a prototype, and gotten our first
external users. Our prototype includes a basic mailer design, a simple cleaning process we
developed in a shared kitchen space, and a first version of the dashboard. We have had a small
number of friends, family and a few local candle makers try the program, and early feedback has
been positive. People said the idea was interesting and that they liked seeing the dashboard.
We have not yet formed a legal entity and we do not have a website. We have not generated
meaningful revenue. Our spending so far has been small and paid by the founders. In the next
year we hope to form a company, sign up several more candle makers, process a few thousand
jars, and begin charging fees. We expect to reach break-even once we have enough partners, but
we have not built a detailed financial model yet.
What We Are Asking For
We are asking for prize funding from the competition to help us take the next steps. We would
use the money to form a legal entity, build a simple website, buy a larger supply of mailers
and cleaning equipment, and run a pilot with more candle makers. We would also like to receive
mentorship and introductions to people in sustainable consumer products, shipping and small
business. Finally, feedback from the judges would help us improve our plan and decide on our
pricing. We believe Wickedgood Candle Return can make reuse easy for candle lovers and help
small makers be more sustainable, and this competition would help us get started.

Question: Share thoughts on market attractiveness and exit potential. Address whether the market would support this venture, whether the company targets the correct group, and whether the market is large enough to support scaling.
